title: Forked Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Non-Markovian Open Quantum Dynamics and Control
authors: Zhao-Wei Wang, Kai-Yu Yuan, Feng-Hua Ren, Zhao-Ming Wang
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a pathway to reunify the simulation and control of quantum systems, in which these two tasks are typically decoupled in traditional strategies. However, most work remains confined to Markovian environments. When applied to non-Markovian systems, standard PINN architectures fail to converge reliably due to multi-objective optimization conflicts arising from the coupled differential equations. To address this fundamental limitation, we extend our previously proposed forked PINN (FPINN) by incorporating a dedicated control branch. By decoupling the optimization objectives at the gradient level via selective gradient flow, our method turns a previously intractable multi-task optimization into a well-conditioned one, allowing simulation and control to be optimized jointly without compromise. Numerical simulations on a two-qubit Heisenberg XXX model confirm that our framework faithfully reproduces the features of non-Markovian dynamics, including decoherence and information backflow. Taking a state-preparation task on the same model as an example, our FPINN achieves higher fidelity than gradient ascent pulse engineering, chopped random basis, and standard PINNs, with the advantage becoming more pronounced as the environment becomes more dissipative and more Markovian. The generated pulses are also noticeably smoother, which is advantageous for experimental implementation. Our framework thus provides a unified, end-to-end differentiable paradigm for simulation and control of open quantum systems, with potential implications for quantum computing, simulation, and control.
summary: This paper introduces the Forked Physics-Informed Neural Network (FPINN) to solve the difficult problem of simulating and controlling open quantum systems under non-Markovian conditions. By selectively decoupling optimization objectives at the gradient level, FPINN overcomes convergence issues faced by standard PINNs in these complex environments. The framework demonstrates superior performance in state preparation fidelity compared to existing optimal control techniques.
main_problem: The core problem is unifying quantum simulation and control for open quantum systems, specifically overcoming the failure of standard Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) when modeling non-Markovian dynamics.
main_result: The proposed Forked PINN (FPINN) successfully achieves joint optimization of simulation and control by decoupling objectives at the gradient level, outperforming established methods like GRAPE in fidelity for state preparation.
method: The authors extend FPINNs by adding a dedicated control branch, utilizing selective gradient flow to transform an intractable multi-task optimization into a well-conditioned one.
model_or_system: The work models open quantum dynamics using the Quantum State Diffusion (QSD) approach for non-Markovian environments. The system is tested on a two-qubit Heisenberg XXX model, governed by master equations involving bath and interaction Hamiltonians.
key_observables: Ground-state population evolution ($P_{00}(t)$), fidelity of state preparation, and the characteristic signatures of information backflow in non-Markovian dynamics.
important_parameters: The memory parameter ($\gamma$) characterizing non-Markovianity, coupling strengths ($\Gamma$), and time-dependent control field amplitudes/frequencies.
main_assumptions: Standard PINNs fail due to multi-objective optimization conflicts when applied to the coupled differential equations arising from non-Markovian dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures compare the simulation of ground-state population ($P_{00}(t)$) using both RK4 (reference) and FPINN across varying dissipation strengths ($\Gamma$) and memory parameters ($\gamma$).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the challenge of non-Markovian PINNs, details the FPINN architecture with its shared trunk and three independent branches, defines a composite loss function ($L_{mod} + L_{tar} + L_{pos}$), and validates the method through numerical simulations on the two-qubit model.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant as it provides an end-to-end differentiable framework for quantum control in realistic, non-Markovian settings, which are crucial for understanding decoherence in physical devices like superconducting qubits or trapped ions.

figures.caption: Figure 1. FPINNs architecture for solving non-markovian open quantum dynamics and control. The input to FPINN is t. The green dashed box denotes the shared layers, which learn common features, while the yellow dashed box denotes the branch layers, which learn unique features. The outputs are feature vector No(t), Nρ(t), and Nc(t). Through reconstruction operations, O(t), ρ(t), and Hs(t) are obtained, and AD is used to compute ∂O/∂t and ∂ρ/∂t. After the gradients of the total loss with respect to the parameters of different branch layers are computed via AD, the updates are performed accordingly.
Figure 2. (a) Evolution of P00(t) simulated by RK4 and FPINN for different Γ. (b) Evolution of P00(t) simulated by RK4 and FPINN for different γ.

Figure 2(b) examines the influence of parameter γ, which characterizes the memory time of the environment. A smaller γ indicates stronger non-Markovianity (longer memory). The simulations fix Γ = 0.3 and vary γ = 0.5, 1, and 2. For smaller γ, the system exhibits a higher degree of recovery at t = π, a hallmark of non-Markovian dynamics where information flows back from the environment to the system. Conversely, larger γ (approaching the Markovian limit) leads to weaker revivals. FPINN faithfully reproduces these features, matching the RK4 reference in all cases.
